key_results: §9.2.1, Eqs. (9.2.2)-(9.2.3), book pp. 397-398: under the standard roundoff model, quantizer error is taken as zero-mean, white, WSS, uniformly distributed over one step, and mutually uncorrelated across quantizers and with the input; the text explicitly warns that deterministic inputs can violate this model.

§9.2.2, Eqs. (9.2.4)-(9.2.5), book pp. 399-400: a quantizer's contribution to output-noise variance equals its source variance multiplied by the energy of its noise transfer function; uncorrelated contributions add in variance.
§9.2.2, book p. 400: increasing fixed-point word length by one bit quarters the quantization-noise variance, an improvement of 6.02 dB.

§9.2.3, book pp. 400-404: scaling can prevent overflow but reduces signal-to-roundoff-noise ratio when internal quantizer noise is unchanged; sum scaling is sufficient for bounded inputs, while L2 scaling is appropriate for finite-energy or WSS analyses.

§9.3, book pp. 405-406: decimation preserves WSS mean and variance and maps autocorrelation as Ryy(k)=Rxx(Mk), whereas expansion generally destroys WSS because output variance becomes periodic in time.
Theorem 9.3.1, book pp. 407-408: if x(n) is white, mutually uncorrelated, zero-mean, and equal-variance (WUZE) and T(z)T~(z)=dI, then y(n)=T(z)x(n) is WUZE with variance multiplied by d.

§9.5.2 and Table 9.5.1, book pp. 413-416: paraunitary structure makes the complete QMF bank's output roundoff noise white and yields simple structure-dependent variance formulas; the M-channel cascaded FIR PR case gains roughly 6.02 dB over the comparable direct two-channel cases when M=2.

§9.6, Eqs. (9.6.3)-(9.6.6), book pp. 416-418: a stable first-order feedback section with |a|<1 and a passive quantizer satisfying |Q(x)|<=|x| cannot sustain zero-input granular or overflow limit cycles; the state magnitude must fall by at least one quantization step until it reaches zero.

§9.7.1, Eq. (9.7.1), book pp. 419-420: in a structurally passive realization whose magnitude cannot exceed unity for any admissible coefficient values, a nominal unity passband extremum can only move downward under coefficient perturbation, so its first-order sensitivity to every coefficient is zero.

§9.7.2, book pp. 421-423: allpass-based power-symmetric IIR QMF banks and FIR PR-QMF lattices retain their bounded/power-complementary structure after admissible multiplier quantization, giving much lower passband sensitivity than direct-form realizations.

Theorem 10.1.1, book pp. 430-432: the M-by-M blocked version of a scalar H(z) is pseudocirculant, its first row is formed from H's Type-1 polyphase components, and it is paraunitary exactly when the scalar filter is allpass.

§10.1.1 and Table 10.1.1, book pp. 429-437: blocking by M runs the matrix filter at one-Mth the sample rate and exposes M-way computational parallelism; a maximally decimated filter bank is alias-free exactly when its polyphase product is pseudocirculant.

§10.1.2 and Table 10.1.1, book pp. 432-437: every equal-rate period-M LPTV system has a maximally decimated filter-bank representation, and it degenerates to an LTI system exactly when the corresponding transfer matrix is pseudocirculant.

§10.2.1, Eqs. (10.2.14)-(10.2.15), book pp. 442-444: the M-fold decimated versions of a sequence and its first M-1 differences form a maximally decimated analysis bank whose binomial-coefficient matrix is self-inverse; FIR synthesis filters of order at most M-1 reconstruct the sequence up to delay.

§10.2.2, book pp. 445-453: if L fixed sample positions are retained from every block of M and x(n) is bandlimited to |omega|<L*pi/M, L multilevel synthesis filters can recover x(n) perfectly in the ideal case; the periodic nonuniform sample pattern has average Nyquist density.

§10.2.2, Eqs. (10.2.30)-(10.2.33), book pp. 447-450: for the two-of-three sample pattern, a lowpass filter controls output amplitude/phase distortion while a Hilbert transformer controls in-band alias cancellation, separating the two approximation errors cleanly.

§11.2.1, book pp. 463-471: evaluating a discrete STFT on M uniformly spaced frequencies is equivalent to an M-channel modulated DFT analysis bank; decimation samples the time-frequency plane, and maximal decimation gives a nonredundant uniform grid.

§11.2.2, Eqs. (11.2.8)-(11.2.12), book pp. 471-473: an STFT can be inverted by integrating over frequency and summing over time shifts when the window-energy normalization is nonzero; the transform coefficients themselves are not unique.

§11.2.3, Eqs. (11.2.15)-(11.2.19), book pp. 473-476: an arbitrary perfect-reconstruction analysis/synthesis filter bank defines a generalized STFT pair, and its shifted synthesis impulse responses are the reconstruction basis; orthonormality becomes a filter-bank correlation condition.
§11.2.4 and Problem 11.6, book pp. 476-481 and 540-541: RMS time and frequency durations obey Dt*Df>=0.5, with equality only for a Gaussian pulse; this quantifies the window-localization tradeoff.

§11.3.1, book pp. 481-487: the wavelet transform follows from two changes to the STFT: generate bandpass filters by dilation rather than uniform modulation, then decimate each band inversely to its bandwidth, producing fine time resolution at high frequency and fine frequency resolution at low frequency.

§11.3.3-§11.3.4, book pp. 491-500: a finite-level discrete wavelet transform is a nonuniform tree filter bank; with FIR analysis/synthesis and perfect reconstruction, its finitely supported basis is complete for arbitrary discrete-time sequences.

Theorem 11.4.1, book p. 506: for an L-level binary perfect-reconstruction tree built from a synthesis pair [Gs(z),Hs(z)], the discrete-time wavelet basis is orthonormal if and only if the pair's 2-by-2 polyphase matrix is paraunitary.

§11.4.3, Eqs. (11.4.21)-(11.4.22), book pp. 508-510: in an M-channel uniform-decimation bank, the discrete-time wavelet basis is orthonormal exactly when the synthesis polyphase matrix is normalized paraunitary.

Lemma 11.5.1, book pp. 528-529: a paraunitary FIR pair generates orthonormal continuous-time wavelets when the autocorrelation of the scaling function is Nyquist(1), equivalently zero at every nonzero integer shift.

Theorem 11.5.1, book p. 530: causal FIR filters of order N generate causal scaling and wavelet functions of duration N; if the pair is paraunitary, |Gs(1)|=sqrt(2), and Gs(e^jomega) has no zero for |omega|<=pi/2, their shifted/dilated wavelets are orthonormal.

§11.5.2-§11.5.3, book pp. 520-530: under the stated paraunitary and lowpass conditions, the finite-duration orthonormal wavelet family is complete over L2(R); paraunitariness alone is insufficient in the infinite-level limit.

§11.5.4, book pp. 530-536: wavelet regularity improves as the lowpass synthesis filter acquires more zeros at omega=pi; for an order-N orthonormal FIR design, at most (N+1)/2 such zeros are possible, achieved through a spectral factor of a maximally flat half-band filter.
Lemma 12.2.1, book pp. 558-559: two nonsingular matrices V1 and V2 generate the same lattice exactly when V1=V2E for an integer unimodular matrix E, formalizing the nonuniqueness of a lattice basis.
§12.2.2, book pp. 559-562: the volume of the fundamental parallelepiped FPD(V) is |det V| and the sampling density is its reciprocal, 1/|det V|.

§12.2.3, Eq. (12.2.30), book pp. 562-568: sampling by V repeats the continuous spectrum at every point of the scaled reciprocal lattice generated by U=2*pi*V^-T; aliasing is overlap among these shifted copies.

§12.3.1-§12.3.2, Eqs. (12.3.5) and (12.3.9), book pp. 568-572: for a 2D circularly supported spectrum, hexagonal sampling packs spectral replicas more tightly than rectangular sampling and lowers the required sample density by a factor of about 1.15.

Division theorem for integer vectors, §12.4.1, book pp. 578-580: for nonsingular integer M, every integer vector has a unique representation n=Mk+r with r in a finite remainder set N(M) of cardinality J(M)=|det M|; this is the indexing foundation for MD polyphase components.
§12.4.1, book pp. 572-580: an M-decimator retains the lattice LAT(M) and changes sample density by J(M)=|det M|; the corresponding expander inserts zeros off that lattice.

§12.4.4, Eqs. (12.4.34)-(12.4.43), book pp. 589-594: generalized orthogonal exponentials indexed by N(M) and N(M^T) form a J(M)-point generalized DFT matrix, extending the ordinary DFT's modulation and orthogonality tools to arbitrary decimation lattices.
§12.5.2, book pp. 599-602: decimation by M is alias-free when the input spectrum is supported in the symmetric parallelepiped SPD(pi*M^-T), or in an equivalent suitably shifted fundamental cell.

§12.6, book pp. 603-608: cascaded decimators compose as M1M2, while the order of matrices matters for expanders and mixed structures; multidimensional noble identities and the polyphase identity move filters across rate changers with matrix-transformed variables.

§12.8.1, book pp. 623-626: a multidimensional Nyquist(M), or M-th-band, filter has a delta-like M-decimated impulse response; equivalently one polyphase component is a delay/constant and the others meet the corresponding zero conditions.

§12.9.1, Eqs. (12.9.1)-(12.9.7), book pp. 627-630: the output of a maximally decimated MD bank is a weighted sum of the desired spectrum and J(M)-1 reciprocal-lattice aliases; alias cancellation is a linear system involving the AC matrix, and perfect reconstruction additionally makes the distortion a pure gain and integer-vector delay.

§12.9.2-§12.9.3, book pp. 631-636: every multidimensional QMF bank reduces to a polyphase product P(z)=R(z)E(z); R(z)E(z)=I yields perfect reconstruction, and unitary-delay cascades give FIR paraunitary PR constructions.

§12.10.1-§12.10.2, book pp. 641-649: Smith-form diagonalization M=U*Lambda*V reduces a general integer decimator to unimodular coordinate changes plus separable one-dimensional rate changes and reveals the generalized DFT as, up to permutations, a Kronecker product of ordinary DFT matrices.
pedagogy: These four advanced chapters repeatedly derive a general matrix/filter-bank result, prove it algebraically, specialize it to familiar structures, and then test it with a concrete design. The teaching style uses equivalent representations as its main explanatory device: random-vector propagation versus losslessness, block filtering versus LPTV versus filter banks, STFT/wavelets versus analysis-synthesis banks, and multidimensional sampling versus lattice geometry. Diagrams are dense and canonical; summary tables consolidate formulas after the derivations. The shard contains 80 problems (13, 8, 23, and 36 by chapter), ranging from short proofs to full synthesis-filter and multidimensional-design constructions. Chapter 9 explicitly assumes fixed-point arithmetic and random-process terminology; Chapters 10-11 assume prior polyphase, PR, and paraunitary filter-bank theory; Chapter 12 adds matrix algebra, determinants, lattices, and vector Fourier/z-transform notation. The treatment is proof-heavy and suitable for an advanced DSP course: intuition comes from geometry and structures, but equations and matrix identities carry the argument. Because the cached source is scan-derived, prose and headings are dependable while any formula intended for publication should be checked against the official page image.

gems: A pole at a=0.99 gives a first-order noise gain of about 50, a sharp numerical reminder that stability alone does not imply benign finite-word behavior. [§9.2.2, Eq. (9.2.6), book p. 400]

One extra fractional bit buys almost exactly 6.02 dB less roundoff-noise variance; Table 9.5.1 then shows an architectural change that can buy the same improvement without adding a bit. [§§9.2.2 and 9.5.2, book pp. 400 and 415-416]

Passive quantization turns a nonlinear feedback argument into a finite countdown: every nonzero first-order state loses at least one step Delta per sample and must hit zero, excluding both granular and overflow limit cycles. [§9.6, book pp. 417-418]

The 6-bit allpass implementation and 8-bit order-23 QMF lattice retain strikingly cleaner passbands than direct-form versions at identical precision, making structural passivity visible rather than merely asserted. [§9.7.2, Figs. 9.7-2 and 9.7-3, book pp. 421-423]

Blocking a scalar filter by M permits an input sample rate M times faster than one computational unit can handle, paid for by M-way parallel hardware; the exact same diagram is an alias-free maximally decimated bank. [§10.1.1, book pp. 428-430]

The first-difference sampler stores 16-bit even samples and 8-bit differences, reducing a slowly varying signal from 16 to an average 12 bits per original sample while retaining exact FIR reconstruction. [§10.2.1, Fig. 10.2-7, book pp. 441-442]

For arbitrary order M, the alternating-binomial difference matrix is its own inverse, so a seemingly exotic sampling theorem reduces to synthesis filters no longer than M. [§10.2.1, Eqs. (10.2.14)-(10.2.20), book pp. 442-444]

The two-of-three nonuniform sampling design reconstructs a length-71 approximately bandlimited sequence with an order-72 lowpass (stopband attenuation above 55 dB) and an order-50 Hilbert transformer. [Design Example 10.2.1, Fig. 10.2-16, book pp. 449-451]

The STFT's best finite symmetric window for concentrating energy in a chosen band is the prolate spheroidal sequence, tying a practical window-design question back to the eigenfilter construction. [§11.2.1, book pp. 468-469]
A Gaussian is not just a customary STFT window: it is the unique waveform that reaches the RMS uncertainty bound Dt*Df=0.5. [§11.2.4 and Problem 11.6, book pp. 477-478 and 540-541]

Design Example 11.4.1 reuses one 23rd-order power-symmetric FIR pair to make both a four-channel equal-band generalized STFT and a three-level octave wavelet bank, with orthonormal bases in both cases. [§11.4.2, Figs. 11.4-2 and 11.4-3, book pp. 506-508]

Replacing z by z^3 in the Haar filters preserves paraunitariness but destroys continuous-time wavelet orthogonality; the counterexample pinpoints why the infinite-level Nyquist(1) condition is genuinely additional. [Example 11.5.6, Figs. 11.5-9 and 11.5-10, book pp. 525-529]

The maximum-regularity construction with K=L=3 starts from an order-10 maximally flat half-band filter and produces an order-5 spectral factor with three zeros at omega=pi. [Design Example 11.5.2, book pp. 535-536]

Packing circular spectra on a hexagonal reciprocal lattice uses six nearest neighbors instead of four and cuts the required sampling density by a factor of about 1.15. [§12.3.2, Figs. 12.3-1 through 12.3-3, book pp. 569-572]
For the support geometry in Fig. 12.4-2, rectangular decimation can reduce density only by two without aliasing, while hexagonal decimation can reduce it by four. [§12.4.1, book pp. 573-575]

The generalized DFT for the chapter's determinant-four hexagonal matrix happens to be exactly the ordinary 4-point DFT up to indexing, but the text immediately warns that this coincidence is not general. [Example 12.4.6, Eq. (12.4.43), book pp. 592-594]

Example 12.7.2 converts rectangular samples directly to a hexagonal lattice—without returning to analog—by interpolating horizontally and then applying a quincunx decimator at unchanged net density. [§12.7.2, Figs. 12.7-3 through 12.7-5, book pp. 612-615]

A quincunx 2D QMF bank inherited from Johnston's 32D one-dimensional prototype reaches a peak distortion of about 0.05 dB, exactly twice the corresponding 1D value. [Example 12.9.3, Fig. 12.9-10, book pp. 637-640]
